result.question:
I have a feeling we keep fixing the same fault on Transformer 1 at site MAIN without ever getting to the root cause. Check that for me.

Pull all closed work orders on Transformer 1 with their number, description, completion date and failure code. Use our failure code catalog to map each one to a transformer fault type: partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, oil overheating, core or winding thermal fault, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing or oil dielectric degradation.

Then work out what the transformer is doing now. Run a dissolved gas fault classification on the latest complete sample between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene, and use co from the same sample to check whether the paper is involved. Map that result to the same list of fault types.

Call it a recurring fault only if at least two closed work orders map to the same fault type the gases show today.

If it's recurring:
- Check open work orders on Transformer 1 for an existing root cause investigation or manufacturer referral. If there is one, give me its number and don't duplicate it.
- Otherwise, create a priority 2 root cause investigation work order. List the earlier work order numbers in the notes, add a note to notify the manufacturer, and code it with the matching failure code.

If only one earlier job matches, don't create anything. Recommend a confirmatory oil resample and say that one repeat isn't enough to call a pattern. If none match, say today's fault looks new.

If a closed work order has no failure code, map it from its description and mark it as inferred. Inferred matches can support a recurrence but can't be the only basis for one. If the latest sample is missing any of the five gases, use the most recent complete sample and give its timestamp.
result.answer:
The DGA interpretation service is down on both attempts, so I've computed the IEC 60599 / Rogers ratios by hand instead. Everything else needed is already in hand, so no further calls are required.

## Verdict: not a recurring fault — today's fault looks new

**Closed work orders on Transformer 1 (site MAIN):** none. I checked the unfiltered list and explicitly for `COMP` and `CLOSE` statuses — there is no completed work history on this asset at all. The only work order on record is an open one (see below). So there are no earlier jobs to map to fault types, coded or inferred.

**Current condition — DGA, sample 2024-01-18T00:00:00** (latest in the window; all five gases present, so no fallback needed):

| Gas | ppm |
|---|---|
| H₂ | 2,900 |
| CH₄ | 7,350 |
| C₂H₆ | 5,450 |
| C₂H₄ | 16,600 |
| C₂H₂ | 7 |
| CO | 33 |

Rogers/IEC ratios (manual, since the `interpret_dga` tool returned "LLM unavailable" twice):
- C₂H₂/C₂H₄ = 0.0004 (< 0.1) → no arcing
- CH₄/H₂ = 2.53 (> 1)
- C₂H₄/C₂H₆ = 3.05 (1–4)

That's IEC fault type **T2 — thermal fault, 300–700 °C**, dominated by ethylene and bordering T3. CO at 33 ppm is very low, so cellulose/paper is **not** involved. Mapped fault type: **oil overheating** (localized thermal fault in the oil, not a core/winding thermal fault and not cellulose ageing).

**Recurrence check:** 0 closed work orders map to oil overheating (0 coded, 0 inferred) — below the two-job threshold. No root cause investigation was created.

**Two things worth flagging anyway:**
1. The gas levels are severe in absolute terms (ethylene 16,600 ppm, methane 7,350 ppm, hydrogen 2,900 ppm are all far above typical IEC 60599 90th‑percentile limits), stable across 15–18 Jan. "New" here means no repair history, not "minor".
2. The existing open WO **1000051** (APPR, priority 1, PdM) — *"OLTC inspection – suspected contact wear/coking"* — already targets this T2 thermal signature and is uncoded because the catalog has no tap-changer failure code. It's an inspection, not a root cause investigation or manufacturer referral, but it's the right first step; I'd let it run and log its findings with a failure code (FC006 – overheating is the closest catalog fit) so future recurrence checks have something to work from.
